title: El Nino, La Nina, IOD and the Himalayan Cryosphere

cards.b:
Climate drivers like El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole decide whether the monsoon fails or floods, and so decide farm output and prices. The Himalayan glaciers feed the great rivers. Prelims asks about definitions and effects. Mains asks about impacts and adaptation.

Learn the two ocean systems and then the glacier story.

ENSO (El Nino-Southern Oscillation) is a cycle in the Pacific. In normal years, trade winds push warm water west, and cold water rises off Peru (the Walker circulation). In an El Nino, trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, and the Peruvian coast warms. Rain shifts east, and Indonesia and India often turn dry.

In La Nina, trade winds strengthen and the eastern Pacific cools. India usually gets good monsoon rain. A year is called El Nino when the sea surface temperature in the Nino 3.4 region stays 0.5 °C above normal for several months. The cycle repeats every 2 to 7 years. The Southern Oscillation Index measures the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin.

El Nino years, such as 2009, 2014, 2015 and 2023, saw weak or deficient monsoon rain, drought risk and higher food prices. Not every El Nino brings a drought, because the Indian Ocean also matters. El Nino also raises global temperatures, and 2023 was a record-warm year. La Nina years bring more rain, floods in the north-east and colder winters in the north.

Farm output, power demand and inflation respond. The IMD and the Ministry of Earth Sciences watch ENSO closely in its monsoon forecasts.

The Indian Ocean Dipole (also the Indian Nino) is the difference in sea surface temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean. A positive IOD (warm west, cool east) favours good Indian monsoon rain and can offset El Nino, as in 1997. A negative IOD can reduce rain. EQUINOO (the Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation) is a related wind pattern.

The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is an eastward-moving pulse of cloud and rain that causes active and break spells of the monsoon in 30 to 60 days. A good monsoon needs a good mix of ENSO, IOD and MJO.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is called the Third Pole because it has the largest ice mass outside the poles. Major glaciers include Gangotri, Siachen (one of the longest outside the poles), Zemu and Pindari. Glaciers feed the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra. Many are retreating faster this century, with black carbon and warming as causes.

Hazards: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). Examples: Kedarnath 2013, Chamoli 2021 (a rock and ice avalanche in the Rishiganga valley) and South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, October 2023. Permafrost thaw destabilises slopes.

In the short term, glacier melt raises river flow, then flow falls once the ice mass is gone ("peak water"). Snow cover, not just glaciers, matters for the Indus basin. India's hill states face more landslides, and the Joshimath subsidence (2023) was a warning.

Tipping points under study include the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), ice sheets and Amazon dieback. Arctic amplification warms the north faster than the rest of the world.

ENSO is a natural cycle, but a warmer world may make El Ninos stronger. Glacier response is mixed: some Karakoram glaciers are stable or growing (the Karakoram anomaly). Critics of dam building in fragile zones say development has outrun science, while states want hydropower and roads.

A balanced answer: improve forecasts, early warning and land-use planning in the mountains.

The National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem (NMSHE) under NAPCC, and the National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change, study these issues. The Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (Goa) monitor ice. Mission Mausam (2024) improves weather forecasting. India runs research stations in Antarctica (Maitri, Bharati) and in the Arctic (Himadri, Svalbard).

• El Nino: warm eastern Pacific; weak monsoon likely.
  • La Nina: cool eastern Pacific; good monsoon.
  • Positive IOD: helps monsoon.
  • GLOF events: 2013, 2021, 2023.
  • Himalaya: the Third Pole.

Also keep the mechanism in one line: weak trade winds, warm east Pacific, shifted rain, weaker Indian monsoon. A single mechanism line often earns the mark.

Prelims-style: "El Nino is characterised by" (warming of the central and eastern Pacific, weakened trade winds). "Positive IOD usually leads to" (good monsoon).

Mains-style: "How do El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole affect the Indian monsoon? Discuss adaptation." Structure: mechanism of each; combined effects; examples of years; farm and economy impact; forecasting and crop planning.
